questions.q: What missing feature of C is the main reason buffer overflows are such a risk in C?
choices: Automatic bounds-checking on array and pointer accesses
Garbage collection of heap memory
Static type checking of function arguments
Support for multi-threaded programs
questions.explain: C does not check bounds automatically. Accessing buf[5] on a char buf[4] raises no error, so checking that every access stays in bounds is up to the programmer.

questions.q: Buffer overflow vulnerabilities only happen in C.
questions.explain: C++ and Objective-C have them too. C is the best-known case because it is so widely used for systems programming.

questions.q: Why is calling gets(buf) on a fixed-size buffer a bug?
choices: gets() keeps storing input for as long as the user keeps supplying it, with no limit tied to the buffer's size
gets() always writes from higher addresses down to lower ones
gets() can only read 4 bytes at a time
gets() frees the buffer after reading
questions.explain: gets() does no bounds checking. If the input is longer than the buffer, it writes past the end of the buffer and overwrites whatever memory comes next.

questions.q: Two globals are declared in this order: char buf[8]; int authenticated = 0; Where is authenticated relative to buf?
choices: At a higher address, directly after buf
At a lower address, directly before buf
On the stack, not in static memory
In the same bytes as buf
questions.explain: Static memory is filled in the order variables are declared and grows upward. buf comes first, so authenticated sits right after it at a higher address, which means an overflow of buf can reach it.

questions.q: Overflowing a static buffer only causes serious harm when security-critical data, like a function pointer or an important flag, sits right after the buffer. That situation is fairly rare in practice.
questions.explain: The text says these conditions occur only rarely. That rarity is why attackers developed more general methods such as stack smashing.

questions.q: What does a function pointer hold?
choices: The address of a function. Calling it jumps to that address and runs the instructions there
A copy of the function's machine code
The function's return value
The number of arguments the function takes
questions.explain: A function pointer is a 4-byte address. If an attacker can change it, the program will start running code from a location the attacker chose.

questions.q: What is the name for an attack that makes a running program execute instructions chosen by the attacker instead of its own code?
questions.explain: When the attack ends, the program is still running, but it is running the attacker's code. If the process ran as root, the attacker now has root's powers.

questions.q: A function has one local array, buf. Going from buf toward higher addresses, which saved values come next in its x86 stack frame?
choices: The sfp (saved ebp), then the rip (saved eip)
The rip, then the sfp
The function's arguments, then the sfp
Nothing; buf is at the top of the stack
questions.explain: The sfp sits right above the local variables, and the rip sits above the sfp. A write that runs past the end of buf hits the sfp first and then the rip.

questions.q: The stack grows down, so gets() writes a local buffer's input from higher addresses to lower addresses.
questions.explain: The stack only grows down when a function call needs new space. Inside a buffer, input is still written from lower addresses to higher ones, toward the sfp and rip.

questions.q: What does the rip (saved eip) in a stack frame hold?
choices: The address of the next instruction to run after the function returns
The caller's saved ebp value
The address of the function's first local variable
The function's return value
questions.explain: When the function returns, execution continues at the address stored in the rip. So if the rip has been corrupted, control goes wherever the corrupted value points.

questions.q: x86 is little-endian. The 4-byte value 0x12345678 is stored in memory. Which byte is at the lowest address?
questions.explain: In little-endian order, the least significant byte goes at the lowest address. So a multi-byte value appears in memory in reverse byte order.

questions.q: Injected malicious code is often written to start an interactive shell for the attacker. What is this kind of code commonly called?
questions.explain: It is called shellcode because it often spawns a shell, which lets the attacker run any commands they want.

questions.q: Which late-1980s worm used a buffer overflow to infect thousands of computers?
choices: The Morris Worm
Code Red
Stuxnet
WannaCry
questions.explain: The Morris Worm dates stack smashing to at least the late 1980s. Code Red came later and used a buffer overflow in the IIS web server to compromise about 369,000 machines.

questions.q: The textbook's rule of thumb: if your program has a buffer overflow bug, assume the bug is exploitable and that an attacker can take control of your program.
questions.explain: Attackers have repeatedly found clever ways to exploit bugs that researchers once thought were too obscure to matter.

questions.q: Why does the C compiler usually not catch a printf call whose format string asks for more arguments than were passed?
choices: printf takes a variable number of arguments, so the compiler only needs at least one, and most compilers do not analyze format strings
The compiler checks the format string, but only for %s
The mismatch only shows up on 64-bit systems
printf counts its arguments at runtime and returns an error
questions.explain: To catch the mismatch, the compiler would need to understand what format modifiers mean, and most compilers do not do that analysis.

questions.q: There are more format modifiers than arguments in a printf call. What does printf do when it reaches the extra modifiers?
choices: It keeps reading values from the stack that were never passed to it, such as leftover data from the previous stack frame
It stops and prints nothing for the missing arguments
It prints zero for each missing argument
It crashes right away with a bounds-check error
questions.explain: printf fetches one argument from the stack for each modifier and does not know how many arguments were actually passed.

questions.q: printf's first argument (the format string) is 4 bytes above printf's RIP. The first %d reads 8 bytes above the RIP, and each later modifier moves 4 bytes higher. How many bytes above the RIP does the third %d read?
questions.explain: The reads go 8, then 12, then 16. If only two arguments were passed, the value at 16 has nothing to do with this call.

questions.q: What does the %n format modifier do?
choices: It treats its argument as an address and writes the number of characters printed so far to that address
It prints a newline
It prints its argument as a character
It prints the string at the address in its argument
questions.explain: %n is the modifier that writes to memory, so a format string vulnerability can overwrite memory as well as leak it.

questions.q: What does the %s format modifier do?
choices: It treats its argument as an address and prints the string at that address up to the first null byte
It prints its argument as a signed integer
It writes the number of characters printed so far
It prints its argument as a single character
questions.explain: %s follows a pointer, so with an attacker-controlled format string it can be used to read memory at other locations.

questions.q: In printf("%d %d %d", x, y, z), the format string's address is at a lower stack address than x, y and z because arguments are pushed in reverse order.
questions.explain: The last argument is pushed first and the first argument is pushed last, so the format string ends up closest to printf's RIP.

questions.q: According to the textbook, what should you assume if a program has a format string vulnerability?
choices: The attacker can learn any value stored in memory and can take control of the program
The attacker can only crash the program
The attacker can only read values in the current stack frame
The bug only matters if the program uses %n
questions.explain: The textbook's bottom line: assume the attacker can both read memory and take control of the program.

questions.q: The code checks if (len > 8) error...; and then calls memcpy(buf, p, len), where len is a signed int from the network and memcpy's third parameter is a size_t (unsigned int). What is the flaw?
choices: A negative len passes the check, then becomes a huge unsigned value when passed to memcpy, which overflows buf
len > 8 should be len >= 8. That is the only bug
memcpy cannot copy from a network string
size_t is signed, so memcpy rejects large values
questions.explain: C silently converts the negative signed value to a large unsigned one. The check looks correct, but it never considers negative values.

questions.q: The C compiler warns about the implicit conversion when a signed int is passed where an unsigned int (size_t) is expected.
questions.explain: The compiler silently inserts the conversion, which is why these bugs are hard to spot.

questions.q: On a 32-bit platform, len is a size_t equal to 0xFFFFFFFF. What is len + 5 (in decimal)?
questions.explain: Unsigned 32-bit arithmetic wraps around. So malloc(len+5) allocates only 4 bytes, and read(fd, buf, len) then writes far more than 4 bytes into it.

questions.q: What makes the code malloc(len+5) followed by read(fd, buf, len) unsafe, even though it allocates 5 extra bytes?
choices: len+5 can wrap around to a small number when len is very large
malloc always rounds the size down
read writes 5 bytes too few
size_t can hold negative values
questions.explain: Integer overflow in the size calculation makes the buffer much smaller than the amount of data written into it. That is a classic buffer overflow.

questions.q: A buffer of size n has bounds checks that are off by one. How many bytes can be written into it?
choices: 2n
Any number
questions.explain: An off-by-one error, such as using <= instead of <, lets exactly one extra byte be written right after the buffer.

questions.q: In the textbook's example (char buf[12] with 13 bytes read in), which value does the extra byte overwrite?
choices: The least significant byte of the saved frame pointer (sfp)
The most significant byte of the rip
The whole rip
The first byte of main()'s local variables
questions.explain: The sfp sits directly above buf. x86 is little-endian, so the byte at the sfp's lowest address is its least significant byte.

questions.q: A one-byte overflow into the sfp cannot be exploited, because it never reaches the rip.
questions.explain: Corrupting one byte of the sfp can lead the program to use a fake stack frame, and that is enough to let an attacker run their own code.

questions.q: When an x86 function returns, which three instructions run, in order?
choices: mov %ebp, %esp, then pop %ebp, then pop %eip
pop %eip, then pop %ebp, then mov %ebp, %esp
pop %ebp, then mov %ebp, %esp, then pop %eip
mov %esp, %ebp, then pop %eip, then pop %ebp
questions.explain: First esp moves to where ebp points (the sfp). Then the saved ebp is popped back into ebp. Then the rip is popped into eip.

questions.q: After the vulnerable function returns with a corrupted sfp, why does the program still go back to main() normally at first?
choices: Only the sfp was changed, so the rip is still correct. The only damage is that ebp now points to the wrong place
The CPU detects the corruption and restores the sfp
The corrupted byte is ignored by pop %ebp
main() never uses ebp
questions.explain: The first return restores a slightly wrong ebp but the correct eip. The effect shows up later, when main() relies on that ebp.

questions.q: Why does an off-by-one into the sfp take a second function return before control is lost?
choices: On its own return, main() uses its corrupted ebp to find its saved ebp and rip, so it reads them from memory it was never meant to use
The first return always crashes, and the operating system restarts the program
The second return overwrites the rip automatically
Each return adds one more byte of overflow
questions.explain: ebp tells a function where its stack frame is. When main() returns, mov %ebp, %esp and the two pops act on the wrong location, so whatever value sits there gets loaded into eip.

questions.q: What is a dangling pointer?
choices: A pointer to a memory region that has been freed and is no longer valid
A pointer that has never been initialized to any value
A pointer to a function
A pointer stored on the heap
questions.explain: Using a dangling pointer is a memory safety violation, because the memory it points to may now be reused for something else.

questions.q: What is a double-free bug?
choices: A dynamically allocated object is explicitly freed more than once
Two pointers point to the same object
An object is allocated twice with malloc
A buffer is overflowed by two bytes
questions.explain: A double free is one of the memory safety violations the textbook lists, alongside using dangling pointers.

questions.q: How are use-after-free bugs generally exploited?
choices: The attacker triggers the creation of a second object that ends up sharing the freed object's memory, then uses the second object to change how the first is interpreted
The attacker frees the stack frame of main()
The attacker overwrites the rip with a format string
The attacker passes a negative length to memcpy
questions.explain: The freed memory is still in use, so a new object placed there overlaps the old one. Changes made through the new object change how the old one is interpreted.

questions.q: In C++, what is an object's vtable pointer?
choices: A pointer to an array of pointers, each holding the address of one of the object's methods
A pointer to the object's first instance variable
The address of the object's constructor only
A count of the object's methods
questions.explain: When a method is called, the program looks up the method's address through the vtable. The object's instance variables are stored directly above the vtable pointer.

questions.q: Overflowing object x's instance variables on the heap overwrites the vtable pointer of object y, which sits above it. How does this differ from overwriting a rip on the stack?
choices: The attacker overwrites a pointer to a pointer, not a direct code address
It only works on the stack
The attacker overwrites the method's machine code directly
It requires a format string bug
questions.explain: The vtable pointer leads to a table of method addresses. So the attacker redirects it to memory they control, which holds the address that will be called.

questions.q: Which of these does the textbook classify as memory safety bugs?
choices: Buffer overflows
Format string vulnerabilities
Using a dangling pointer
Double-free bugs
Choosing a weak password
questions.explain: Memory safety bugs let an attacker read or write beyond the valid range of memory regions, or misuse memory that has been freed. A weak password is a different kind of problem.
